ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 2

Concurrent Executions
•Concurrent execution means that multiple transactions are executed 
simultaneously in an interleaved(mixed) manner.
•When multiple transactions execute concurrently without proper control, it 
may lead to problems affecting data integrity and consistency. 
•Such issues are called Concurrency Problems (or Anomalies).
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 3

Concurrency Problems
1. Lost Update (Write–Write Conflict)
2. Uncommitted Data / Dirty Read (Write–Read Conflict)
3. Inconsistent Retrieval / Unrepeatable Read (Read–Write Conflict)
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 4

Concurrent Executions
Solution
To ensure correctness, DBMS enforces:
Serializability
Concurrent schedule must produce the same result as some serial schedule
Concurrency Control Techniques
•Locking (2PL – Two Phase Locking) 
•Timestamp Ordering 
•Validation-based protocols
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 5

Concurrency Control
• The system must control the interaction among the concurrent transactions.
• This control is achieve through one of concurrency control schemes.
• Concurrency control is a fundamental concept in database systems that ensures 
correct execution of simultaneous transactions without violating data integrity. 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 6

Concurrency Control
Below are some characteristics of concurrency control:
•It enforces isolation among transactions. Transactions do not interfere with each 
other. Each transaction behaves as if it is executed alone
•It preserves database consistency through consistency preserving execution of 
transactions. Ensures only valid data states are produced. Executes transactions in 
a consistency-preserving manner
•It resolves read-write and write-read conflicts. Handles read–write conflicts. 
Handles write–read conflicts. Prevents issues like dirty reads, lost updates, etc.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 7

Concurrency Control protocols
Various concurrency control techniques are:
➢Lock-based Protocols 
➢Time stamp-based Protocols
➢Validation-based Protocols
Locking is one of the most widely used mechanisms.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 8

Lock-Based Protocols 
• To ensure isolation, it is required that data items should be accessed in mutual 
exclusive manner.
• If one transaction is accessing a data item, no other transaction can modify that 
data item. 
• A lock is a mechanism to control concurrent access to a data item
• A transaction is allowed to access a data item only if it is currently holding a 
lock on that item.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 9

Lock-Based Protocols 
Modes of lock:
1. Shared Lock (S) 
❖If a transaction Ti has obtained a shared-mode lock (denoted by S) on item Q, 
then Ti can read, but cannot write, Q.
❖ S-lock is requested using lock-S instruction.
2. Exclusive Lock (X) 
❖If a transaction Ti has obtained an exclusive-mode lock (denoted by X) on item 
Q, then Ti can both read and write Q.
❖X-lock is requested using lock-X instruction.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 10

Lock-Based Protocols 
• We require that every transaction request a lock in an appropriate mode on data 
item Q, depending on the types of operations that it will perform on Q.
• The transaction makes the request to the concurrency-control manager.
• The transaction can proceed with the operation only after the concurrency￾control manager grants the lock to the transaction.
• The use of these two lock modes allows multiple transactions to read a data item 
but limits write access to just one transaction at a time.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 11

Lock-Based Protocols 
Compatibility Function:
• Let A and B represent arbitrary lock modes. 
• Suppose that a transaction Ti requests a lock of mode A on item Q on which 
transaction Tj (Ti = Tj ) currently holds a lock of mode B.
• If transaction Ti can be granted a lock on Q immediately, in spite of the presence 
of the mode B lock, then we say mode A is compatible with mode B.
Lock Compatibility Matrix:
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 12

Lock-Based Protocols 
• A transaction may be granted a lock on an item if the requested lock is 
compatible with locks already held on the item by other transactions.
• Any number of transactions can hold shared locks on an item, 
• But if any transaction holds an exclusive on the item no other transaction may hold 
any lock on the item.
• If a lock cannot be granted, the requesting transaction is made to wait till all 
incompatible locks held by other transactions have been released. The lock is 
then granted.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 13

Lock-Based Protocols

• Locking as above is not sufficient to guarantee serializability — if A and B get updated 
in-between the read of A and B, the displayed sum would be wrong.
• A locking protocol is a set of rules followed by all transactions while requesting and 
releasing locks. Locking protocols restrict the set of possible schedules.

Two-Phase Locking (2PL) Protocol 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 16

Two-Phase Locking (2PL) Protocol 
Lock Conversions
• Two-phase locking protocol with lock conversions:
 – Growing Phase: 
◦ can acquire a lock-S on item
◦ can acquire a lock-X on item
◦ can convert a lock-S to a lock-X (upgrade)
 – Shrinking Phase:
◦ can release a lock-S
◦ can release a lock-X
◦ can convert a lock-X to a lock-S (downgrade)
• This protocol ensures serializability.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 17

Two-Phase Locking (2PL) Protocol 
• Two-phase locking does not ensure freedom from deadlocks.
• In addition to deadlocks, there is a possibility of starvation.
• Extensions to basic two-phase locking needed to ensure recoverability of freedom 
from cascading roll-back.
• Strict two-phase locking: a transaction must hold all its exclusive locks till it 
commits/aborts.
• Ensures recoverability and avoids cascading roll-backs
• Rigorous two-phase locking: a transaction must hold all locks till commit/abort. 
• Transactions can be serialized in the order in which they commit.
• Most databases implement rigorous two-phase locking, but refer to it as simply 
two-phase locking.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 21

Two-Phase Locking (2PL) Protocol 
Implementation of Locking
• A lock manager can be implemented as a separate process.
•Transactions can send lock and unlock requests as messages.
•The lock manager replies to a lock request by sending a lock grant messages (or a 
message asking the transaction to roll back, in case of a deadlock).
•The requesting transaction waits until its request is answered.
•The lock manager maintains an in-memory data-structure called a lock table to 
record granted locks and pending requests.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 22

Two-Phase Locking (2PL) Protocol 
Three Activities in 2PL
•Lock Acquisition :Transaction obtains required locks. 
•Modification of Data: Performs read/write operations. 
•Release Lock : Frees the locks after completion.
Key Points
•Ensures conflict serializability. 
•Maintains data consistency.
•May still lead to deadlocks and starvation.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 23

Deadlock
• Consider the partial schedule:
•Neither T3 nor T4 can make progress —
executing lock-S(B) causes T4 to wait for T3 
to release its lock on B, while executing lock￾X(A) causes T3 to wait for T4 to release its 
lock on A. 
• Such a situation is called a deadlock.
• To handle a deadlock one of T3 or T4 must be 
rolled back and its locks released. 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 24

Timestamp-Based Protocols
•Timestamp-based protocols are concurrency control techniques that use timestamps instead 
of locks to ensure correct execution of transactions. Each transaction is assigned a unique 
timestamp when it starts, which determines its order.
•In the Timestamp Ordering Protocol, all operations must follow the chronological order of 
timestamps. If a transaction tries to read or write a data item in a way that violates this order, 
the transaction is rolled back and restarted with a new timestamp.
•This protocol maintains two timestamps for each data item: read timestamp (RTS) and write 
timestamp (WTS). These are used to decide whether an operation is allowed or should be 
rejected.
•The main advantage of timestamp-based protocols is that they are deadlock-free, since 
transactions do not wait for locks. However, they may lead to frequent rollbacks, which can 
reduce performance in high-contention systems.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 25

Timestamp-Based Protocols
• Each transaction is issued a timestamp when it enters the system. 
• If an old transaction Ti has time-stamp TS(Ti), a new transaction Tj is assigned time￾stamp TS(Tj) such that TS(Ti) <TS(Tj). 
• The protocol manages concurrent execution such that the time-stamps determine the 
serializability order.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 26

Timestamp-Based Protocols
• In order to assure such behavior, the protocol maintains for each data Q two 
timestamp values:
• W-timestamp(Q) is the largest time-stamp of any transaction that executed write(Q) 
successfully.
• R-timestamp(Q) is the largest time-stamp of any transaction that executed read(Q) 
successfully.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 27

Timestamp-Based Protocols
• The timestamp ordering protocol ensures that any conflicting read and write 
operations are executed in timestamp order.
• Suppose a transaction Ti issues a read(Q):
1. If TS(Ti) < W-timestamp(Q), then Ti needs to read a value of Q that was already 
overwritten. Hence, the read operation is rejected, and Ti is rolled back.
2. If TS(Ti)  W-timestamp(Q), then the read operation is executed, and R￾timestamp(Q) is set to max(R-timestamp(Q), TS(Ti)).
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 28

Timestamp-Based Protocols
•Suppose a transaction Ti issues a write(Q):
1. If TS(Ti) < R-timestamp(Q), then the value of Q that Ti is producing was needed 
previously, and the system assumed that that value would never be produced. 
Hence, the write operation is rejected, and Ti is rolled back.
2. If TS(Ti) < W-timestamp(Q), then Ti is attempting to write an obsolete value of 
Q. Hence, this write operation is rejected, and Ti is rolled back.
3. Otherwise, the write operation is executed, and W-timestamp(Q) is set to TS(Ti).
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 29

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 30
Important terms:
oSmaller TS → Older transaction
oLarger TS → Younger transaction
All operations must follow timestamp order
If order is violated → transaction is rolled back (aborted)
▪ RTS (Read Timestamp): Latest time a data item was read 
▪WTS (Write Timestamp): Latest time a data item was written 
Used to decide whether an operation is allowed or not
Deadlock Prevention using Timestamps
1. Wait-Die Scheme (Non-Preemptive)
2. Wound-Wait Scheme (Preemptive)

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 36

Correctness of Timestamp-Ordering Protocol
• The timestamp-ordering protocol guarantees serializability since all the arcs in the 
precedence graph are of the form:
• Thus, there will be no cycles in the precedence graph
• Timestamp protocol ensures freedom from deadlock as no transaction ever waits. 
• But the schedule may not be cascade-free, and may not even be recoverable.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 37

Timestamp-Ordering Protocol
Recoverability and Cascade Freedom
Problem with timestamp-ordering protocol:
• Suppose Ti aborts, but Tj has read a data item written by Ti.
• Then Tj must abort; if Tj had been allowed to commit earlier, the schedule is not 
recoverable.
• Further, any transaction that has read a data item written by Tj must abort.
• This can lead to cascading rollback --- that is, a chain of rollbacks.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 38

Timestamp-Ordering Protocol
Recoverability and Cascade Freedom
Solution 1:
• A transaction is structured such that its writes are all performed at the end of its 
processing.
• All writes of a transaction form an atomic action; no transaction may execute while a 
transaction is being written.
• A transaction that aborts is restarted with a new timestamp.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 39

Timestamp-Ordering Protocol
Recoverability and Cascade Freedom
Solution 2:
• Limited form of locking: wait for data to be committed before reading it.
Solution 3:
• Use commit dependencies to ensure recoverability.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 40

Thomas’ Write Rule
• Modified version of the timestamp-ordering protocol in which obsolete write
operations may be ignored under certain circumstances.
• When Ti attempts to write data item Q, if TS(Ti) < W-timestamp(Q), then Ti is 
attempting to write an obsolete value of {Q}. 
• Rather than rolling back Ti as the timestamp ordering protocol would have done, 
this {write} operation can be ignored.
• Otherwise, this protocol is the same as the timestamp ordering protocol.
• Thomas' Write Rule allows greater potential concurrency. 
• allows some view-serializable schedules that are not conflict-serializable.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 41

Validation-Based Protocol
• Execution of transaction Ti is done in three phases.
1. Read and execution phase: Transaction Ti writes only to temporary local variables
2. Validation phase: Transaction Ti performs a ''validation test'' to determine if local 
variables can be written without violating serializability.
3. Write phase: If Ti is validated, the updates are applied to the database; otherwise, Ti 
is rolled back.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 42

Validation-Based Protocol
• The three phases of concurrently executing transactions can be interleaved, but each 
transaction must go through the three phases in that order.
• Assume for simplicity that the validation and write phase occur together, atomically 
and serially
• i.e., only one transaction executes validation/write at a time. 
• Also called as optimistic concurrency control since transaction executes fully in the 
hope that all will go well during validation.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 43

Validation-Based Protocol
• Each transaction Ti has 3 timestamps
• Start(Ti) : the time when Ti started its execution
• Validation(Ti): the time when Ti entered its validation phase
• Finish(Ti) : the time when Ti finished its write phase
• Serializability order is determined by timestamp given at validation time; this is done 
to increase concurrency. 
• Thus, TS(Ti) is given the value of Validation(Ti).
•This protocol is useful and gives greater degree of concurrency if probability of 
conflicts is low. 
• because the serializability order is not pre-decided, and
• relatively few transactions will have to be rolled back.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 44

Validation Test for Transaction Tj
• If for all Ti with TS (Ti) < TS (Tj) either one of the following condition holds:
• finish(Ti) < start(Tj) 
• start(Tj) < finish(Ti) < validation(Tj) and the set of data items written by Ti does not 
intersect with the set of data items read by Tj. 
• then validation succeeds and Tj can be committed. Otherwise, validation fails and Tj
is aborted.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 45

Validation Test for Transaction Tj
Justification: 
Either the first condition is satisfied, and there is no overlapped execution, or the second 
condition is satisfied and
• the writes of Tj do not affect reads of Ti since they occur after Ti has finished its reads.
• the writes of Ti do not affect reads of Tj since Tj does not read any item written by Ti.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 46

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 47

Deadlock
• System is deadlocked if there is a set of transactions such that every transaction 
in the set is waiting for another transaction in the set.
• Thus, the transactions are waiting indefinitely for each other to release locks, 
and none of them can proceed. 
• This commonly occurs in lock-based protocols when transactions hold some 
resources and wait for others.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 48

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 49
Step Transaction T₁ Transaction T₂
1 Lock-X(A)
2 Lock-X(B)
3 Lock-X(B) (Wait)
4 Lock-X(A) (Wait)
Deadlock Example
•T₁ holds A and wants B
•T₂ holds B and wants A
Both are waiting for each other
Deadlock occurs
Circular wait = Deadlock
Solution
•Abort (rollback) one transaction 
•Or use prevention (wait-die / wound-wait) 
Schedule S:

Necessary Conditions of Deadlock 
For a deadlock to occur in a DBMS, all four conditions must be true simultaneously:
1. Mutual Exclusion
Only one transaction can hold a resource (lock) at a time . Other transactions must wait if 
the resource is already locked 
2. Hold and Wait
A transaction is holding one resource .While waiting for another resource held by another 
transaction 
3. No Preemption
Resources (locks) cannot be forcibly taken away .They are released only by the transaction 
itself
4. Circular Wait
A cycle of transactions exists . Each transaction is waiting for a resource held by the next
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 50

Deadlock Handling
There are three main approaches to handle deadlocks. 
•The first is deadlock prevention, where the system ensures that deadlocks never occur by 
restricting how locks are requested. Techniques like wait-die and wound-wait use timestamps to 
decide which transaction should wait or be rolled back.
•The second approach is deadlock avoidance, where the system checks whether granting a lock 
request will lead to a deadlock. If there is a risk, the request is denied. This approach is less 
commonly used due to its complexity.
•The third approach is deadlock detection and recovery. In this method, the system allows 
deadlocks to occur but periodically checks for them using a wait-for graph. If a cycle is found, 
one transaction is selected as a victim and rolled back to break the deadlock.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 51

Deadlock Prevention Techniques
They are:
•Wait-Die Protocol
•Wound-Wait Protocol
Both are timestamp-based deadlock prevention algorithms
When multiple transactions run together, they may get into a deadlock (each waiting for the 
other forever).
•These protocols prevent deadlock before it happens
They decide: who should wait and who should be aborted
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 52

Wait-Die Scheme
In this protocol, if a transaction requests to lock a resource (data item), which is already held 
with a conflicting lock by another transaction, then one of the two possibilities may occur − 
• If TS(Ti) < TS(Tj) − that is Ti, which is requesting a conflicting lock, is older than Tj − then Ti is 
allowed to wait until the data-item is available. 
• If TS(Ti) > TS(tj) − that is Ti is younger than Tj − then Ti dies. Ti is restarted later with a random 
delay but with the same timestamp. 
•This scheme allows the older transaction to wait but kills the younger one. 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 53

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 54
Assume two transactions:
T1 with timestamp TS(T1) = 5 (older) 
T2 with timestamp TS(T2) = 10 (younger) 
Smaller timestamp = older transaction
Case 1: Older transaction requests a lock 
(WAIT)
•T2 already holds a lock on data item X
•Now T1 requests a lock on X
Check condition:
•TS(T1) < TS(T2) → 5 < 10 
• (T1 is older) 
According to Wait-Die:
•T1 is allowed to WAIT
Result:
•T1 waits until T2 releases the lock 
•No transaction is killed
Case 2: Younger transaction requests a lock 
(DIE)
•T1 already holds a lock on data item X
•Now T2 requests a lock on X
Check condition:
•TS(T2) > TS(T1) → 10 > 5 
•(T2 is younger) 
According to Wait-Die:
•T2 will DIE (abort)
Result:
•T2 is rolled back 
•Later, T2 restarts with same timestamp (10)
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 55

Wound-Wait Scheme
In this protocol, if a transaction requests to lock a resource (data item), which is already held 
with conflicting lock by some another transaction, one of the two possibilities may occur −
• If TS(Ti) < TS(Tj), then Ti forces Tj to be rolled back − that is Ti wounds Tj. Tj is restarted later 
with a random delay but with the same timestamp.
• If TS(Ti) > TS(Tj), then Ti is forced to wait until the resource is available. 
This protocol, allows the younger transaction to wait; but when an older transaction requests an 
item held by a younger one, the older transaction forces the younger one to abort and release 
the item.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 56

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 57
Assume:
T1 → TS = 5 (older)
T2 → TS = 10 (younger)
Case 1: Older transaction requests lock → 
WOUND
•T2 (younger) is holding lock on data item X
•T1 (older) requests lock on X
Check condition:
•TS(T1) < TS(T2) → 5 < 10 
•(T1 is older) 
According to Wound-Wait:
•T1 wounds T2 , T2 is aborted
Result:
•T2 is rolled back immediately 
•Lock on X is released 
•T1 gets the lock
Case 2: Younger transaction requests lock → 
WAIT
•T1 (older) is holding lock on data item X
•T2 (younger) requests lock on X
Check condition:
•TS(T2) > TS(T1) → 10 > 5 (T2 is younger) 
According to Wound-Wait:
•T2 is allowed to WAIT
Result:
•T2 waits until T1 releases the lock 
•No abort happens
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 58

Deadlock Detection
• Deadlocks can be described as a wait-for graph, which consists of a pair G = 
(V,E),
◦ V is a set of vertices (all the transactions in the system)
◦ E is a set of edges; each element is an ordered pair Ti →Tj
.
• If Ti → Tj is in E, then there is a directed edge from Ti to Tj, implying that Ti is 
waiting for Tj to release a data item.
• When Ti requests a data item currently being held by Tj, then the edge Ti → Tj is 
inserted in the wait-for graph. This edge is removed only when Tj is no longer 
holding a data item needed by Ti. 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 59

Deadlock Detection
• The system is in a deadlock state if and only if the wait-for graph has a cycle. 
• Must invoke a deadlock-detection algorithm periodically to look for cycles.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 60
Wait-for graph without a cycle Wait-for graph with a cycle

Deadlock Recovery
• When deadlock is detected:
• Some transaction will have to rolled back (made a victim) to break deadlock. Select 
that transaction as victim that will incur minimum cost.
• Rollback -- determine how far to roll back transaction.
• Total rollback: Abort the transaction and then restart it.
• More effective to roll back transaction only as far as necessary to break deadlock.
• Starvation happens if same transaction is always chosen as victim. Include the 
number of rollbacks in the cost factor to avoid starvation.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 61
